cards.statement: Migrate to Virtual Machines can create a test clone for validation while the source workload stays live.
cards.explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines builds a test clone from replicated data. A team validates that separate clone while the source continues serving traffic.

cards.statement: Apigee's Quota policy can pace an application's permitted API calls evenly over the quota measurement interval.
cards.explanation: Apigee's Quota policy counts requests over its configured interval. A client can consume its allowance in a burst; SpikeArrest handles traffic-spike protection.
cards.misconception: A request quota spaces an application's allowed calls evenly through the quota period.

cards.statement: Apigee hybrid processes API traffic in the runtime plane hosted in a customer-managed Kubernetes cluster.
cards.explanation: Apigee hybrid's runtime services handle API calls in the customer's Kubernetes environment. That runtime boundary keeps API traffic processing under the customer's network control.

cards.statement: Migrate to Virtual Machines supports Google Cloud VMware Engine as the destination for on-premises vSphere VMs.
cards.explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines accepts Google Cloud VMware Engine as a source and moves VM workloads into Compute Engine. VMware Engine is a source platform in this migration path.
cards.misconception: Migrate to Virtual Machines targets VMware Engine rather than Compute Engine for on-premises vSphere migrations.

cards.statement: Google recommends continuing PostgreSQL source writes while promoting a continuous Database Migration Service job.
cards.explanation: Google's PostgreSQL migration guidance stops source writes and waits for replication lag to reach zero before promotion. This makes the destination the primary database at cutover.
cards.misconception: A continuous database migration preserves source writes through destination promotion.

source.title: Migrate a database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL by using Database Migration Service

cards.statement: Storage Transfer Service's checksum validation confirms that a copied file is the latest version at the source.
cards.explanation: Storage Transfer Service validates transferred data using available checksums. Google recommends separate checks for the correct file version when files change at the source.
cards.misconception: A successful transfer checksum proves that the destination holds the latest source version.

cards.statement: Transfer Appliance keeps EU customers' offline data transfers within the EU when they choose an EU destination region.
cards.explanation: Google handles EU customers' Transfer Appliance shipping and data upload through Belgium. An EU destination region keeps the transfer process within EU boundaries.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer Appliance logistics and regional processing arrangements can change.

cards.statement: Datastream preserves source commit order as it delivers change events into Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Datastream delivers change events that can arrive out of order. A Cloud Storage consumer uses source-specific event metadata to reconstruct the source operation order.
cards.misconception: Datastream guarantees source commit order in the sequence of delivered change events.

cards.statement: Google recommends production-like pre-production GKE environments for application integration testing.
cards.explanation: Google's GKE guidance aligns pre-production and production conditions to reduce failures caused by environmental differences. Pre-production clusters may be scaled down for cost.

source.title: Best practices for continuous integration and delivery to Google Kubernetes Engine

cards.statement: Gemini Cloud Assist can refine Terraform code through conversations about a team's infrastructure requirements.
cards.explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist iteratively generates or refines Terraform through interactive infrastructure discussions. Google recommends validating its generated output before use.
cards.volatilityNote: Gemini Cloud Assist is a Preview offering whose infrastructure assistance can change.

cards.statement: Google recommends attached service account credentials for Application Default Credentials in Google Cloud production.
cards.explanation: Google's production guidance favors the service account attached to the compute resource. The application obtains credentials from its environment rather than carrying a key file.

cards.statement: Application Default Credentials prioritizes an attached service account over a credential file set in the environment.
cards.explanation: Application Default Credentials checks the environment-specified credential file before the attached service account. A file left in the environment can change which identity a deployed workload uses.
cards.misconception: An attached service account takes precedence over an environment-specified credential file.

cards.statement: Reusing a Google Cloud client library session can reduce repeated authentication work across requests.
cards.explanation: A Google Cloud session client reuses cached access tokens while they remain valid. Google recommends reusing client objects for requests made with the same credentials.

cards.statement: BigQuery's Cloud Client Libraries automatically fetch remaining result pages before an application begins iteration.
cards.explanation: BigQuery client iterators retrieve further pages as iteration needs them. Automatic pagination hides page requests from application code rather than fetching the full result up front.
cards.misconception: Automatic pagination eagerly fetches the complete result before iteration starts.

source.title: Using pagination with the BigQuery API

cards.statement: Retrying Cloud Storage's Pub/Sub notification creation after a timeout can create duplicate configurations.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage creates a fresh notification ID on each successful creation request. A timeout can hide a successful first attempt, so retrying that call can add another configuration.

cards.statement: The Bigtable emulator preserves test data on local disk so a later emulator process can reuse it.
cards.explanation: The Bigtable emulator keeps its data in memory and loses it across runs. Tests that need an initial dataset populate that dataset for a new emulator run.
cards.misconception: The Bigtable emulator persists application data on local disk between processes.

cards.statement: Google API Client Libraries can use gRPC for an integration with an API that offers REST and gRPC.
cards.explanation: Google API Client Libraries expose REST. An integration that needs gRPC uses a gRPC-capable Cloud Client Library or a generated gRPC client instead.
cards.misconception: Google API Client Libraries provide gRPC transport when the API exposes it.

source.title: Client libraries and Cloud APIs explained

cards.statement: Infrastructure Manager keeps a Terraform state file with each deployment revision's metadata.
cards.explanation: Infrastructure Manager stores Terraform state alongside revision metadata. A team can inspect a particular revision's state when investigating past infrastructure changes.

cards.statement: Config Connector corrects drift in declared readable, mutable fields through periodic reconciliation by default.
cards.explanation: Config Connector treats the declared configuration as the desired state. Later reconciliations can overwrite direct changes to readable, mutable fields, so external edits can compete with it.

cards.statement: Cloud Shell's VM automatically joins the selected project's VPC network for private resource access.
cards.explanation: Google hosts the Cloud Shell VM outside the customer's VPC network. Selecting a project leaves that network boundary in place, so private IP access needs a separate connectivity path.
cards.misconception: Selecting a project places the Cloud Shell VM in that project's VPC network.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework recommends addressing operational requirements during architecture design.
cards.explanation: Google's operational excellence pillar includes operational requirements in the architect's design and implementation work. Operational efficiency and scalability belong in the initial solution design.

cards.statement: Google's example error budget policy allows routine feature releases while a service exceeds its error budget.
cards.explanation: Google's example error budget policy halts routine changes after the service exceeds its budget. Critical incident and security fixes are exceptions while the team restores SLO compliance.
cards.misconception: An exhausted error budget leaves routine feature releases proceeding as usual.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can warn of rapid SLO error-budget consumption while the service still has budget remaining.
cards.explanation: Cloud Monitoring burn-rate alerts evaluate the rate of error-budget consumption. A fast-burn alert warns of sustained errors that would soon exhaust the budget, giving operators time to respond.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging sinks route matching entries received after sink creation to the configured destination.
cards.explanation: Cloud Logging evaluates sinks as entries arrive. Creating a sink leaves earlier stored entries in their original storage rather than replaying them to the new destination.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets analysts update log entries through a dataset linked to a Cloud Logging bucket.
cards.explanation: A linked BigQuery dataset gives read access to log data stored by Cloud Logging. Analysts query that data through BigQuery, while the linked dataset leaves the original log entries unchanged.
cards.misconception: Linking a log bucket to BigQuery enables analysts to modify the source log entries.

source.title: Create a linked BigQuery dataset on a log bucket

cards.statement: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus limits PromQL query results to a single Google Cloud region.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus evaluates queries against a global datastore and combines results across regions. Teams obtain a unified view rather than querying isolated regional servers.
cards.misconception: Managed Prometheus query evaluation is confined to one regional datastore.
tags: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

source.title: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

cards.statement: Cloud Trace can directly apply tail-based sampling to incoming spans using a completed request's latency.
cards.explanation: Cloud Trace receives spans selected by sending components. Tail-based selection needs an upstream component, such as an OpenTelemetry Collector, to choose which spans to send.
cards.misconception: Cloud Trace performs tail-based selection after receiving the completed trace.

cards.statement: Cloud Profiler can automatically sample production CPU usage to identify expensive application code paths.
cards.explanation: Cloud Profiler attributes sampled resource use to application source code with low overhead. Profiling in production exposes resource consumption under the workload's real operating conditions.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can run private uptime checks against a VPC in a project outside its metrics scope.
cards.explanation: For private uptime checks, the Service Directory service belongs in the metrics scope. The VPC and resources represented by that service may reside in another project outside the scope.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring retains elapsed retest time when a metric-threshold alert condition briefly clears.
cards.explanation: For Cloud Monitoring metric-threshold alerts, a nonviolating measurement resets the retest window. A brief recovery restarts the wait rather than preserving the elapsed violation time.
cards.misconception: Separate threshold-violation bursts accumulate toward one retest window.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy advances canary phases across regional targets through their shared controller rollout.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Deploy multi-target rollout advances its child rollouts when the controller advances. This coordinates progressive deployment across regional targets.

cards.statement: Cloud Run rolls back a service by routing traffic to a retained revision rather than rebuilding its container image.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run restores an existing revision by changing traffic allocation. Keeping the prior revision available gives the team a routing-based rollback path.

source.title: Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration

cards.statement: Compute Engine exempts temporary MIG rolling-update VMs from the project's resource quotas.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine needs available quota and capacity for a MIG's extra update VMs. A release plan that uses temporary replacement VMs needs that resource headroom.
cards.misconception: Temporary VMs used for rolling updates are exempt from the resource quotas that constrain ordinary VMs.

source.title: Automatically apply VM configuration updates in a MIG

cards.statement: Cloud Run resets a service's traffic split to the latest revision by default after another deployment.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run preserves an existing traffic split pattern across subsequent deployments. A team changes the traffic allocation explicitly to return traffic to the latest revision.
cards.misconception: Another deployment clears an existing traffic split and restores the latest revision as the sole traffic destination.

source.title: Rollbacks, gradual rollouts, and traffic migration

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy automatically creates a new rollout from an earlier release when a team rolls back a target.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Deploy rollback creates another rollout associated with a previous release. The rollback is a new deployment action rather than an edit to the earlier rollout.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy automatically marks a rollout as failed when post-deployment verification reports failure.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy runs the team's verification tests after deployment. Failed verification fails the rollout, giving the team a quality gate before treating that delivery as successful.

cards.statement: Google's incident model assigns hands-on mitigation to the Incident Commander after appointing an Ops Lead.
cards.explanation: In Google's incident model, the Ops Lead applies operational tools to mitigate the incident. The Incident Commander coordinates the response and delegates responsibilities.
cards.misconception: The Incident Commander remains the hands-on remediation lead after an Ops Lead takes that role.

cards.statement: Google recommends combining failure simulations with load testing to assess behavior during real usage.
cards.explanation: Google's recovery testing guidance adds realistic request load to simulated outages. This tests how the system behaves when failures happen while users are active.

source.title: Perform testing for recovery from failures

cards.statement: Google Cloud requires notification before penetration testing that affects just a customer's own projects.
cards.explanation: Google permits penetration testing of a customer's projects without prior contact. The tester follows the Acceptable Use Policy and Terms of Service and confines effects to their own projects.
cards.misconception: A tester needs to notify Google before a penetration test limited to the tester's own projects.

cards.statement: Google recommends isolating a Spanner load test from other services when validating production peak capacity.
cards.explanation: Google's Spanner launch checklist includes interacting services and realistic user journeys in load tests. Isolated database tests miss competing application and background workloads.
cards.misconception: An isolated database benchmark is Google's recommended way to validate peak capacity for a production Spanner application.
